title: ‘I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it’: Kate Courtney interview
content:
Cyclist
‘I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it’: Kate Courtney interview

Cyclist: You made your name in mountain biking. Why the switch to road?

Kate Courtney: It’s really about what excites me. I think there are certain goals in life that keep you up at night and speak to you, and for me right now that’s road.

How did the FDJ United-Suez link come about?

When I started considering the switch, things escalated very quickly. I don’t have an intermediate setting as a person, I’m a zero-to-100 girl, and this certainly followed that trend. I started to talk to everyone I knew involved in the sport who might have advice on what I would need to do to make the jump to the next level and where might be the right fit to make that jump. It came about really organically. It was clear from the beginning that the team would be a great fit.

Have you already moved from the US to Europe?

Not for this year. I’m currently based in California, just south of San Francisco, but next year I will certainly split my time between home and Europe with the team quite a bit. I’m looking at some potential spots to base myself – it’s likely going to be Spain like all the other American cyclists.

You went to Belgium recently for experience and ended up winning two races. What were you able to take away from that?

Kermesse racing is such a historic staple of the road development pathway in Europe, so I went to learn and pay homage to the origins of the sport and to these races. The biggest takeaway was learning to apply the skills I already have. The first day was honestly terrifying. I found myself in the back of a bar, signing up for what is essentially a crit race for over 100 girls. It was a mixture of all the things that I would say are weaknesses coming to the road, like bunch dynamics, wind, cobbles, cracks and the near certainty of a sprint finish.

I was actually pretty comfortable in the bunch and loved it. I used a lot of the skills that I have from mountain biking – bunny-hopping a rock, for example, is not that different from bunny-hopping a crack on the road in Belgium. The more I’m exposed to these types of opportunities that match my skill level the more I gain in confidence. That’s going to be the most important thing for stepping up to the next level and not just being there to participate but to really compete.

What kind of races do you see yourself targeting?

We’ll see, and that’s an exciting thing. This is an exploratory phase to see where I thrive on the road. The spring Classics and making a Grand Tour team next year would be big goals. Stephen [Delcourt, team manager] calls me his junior on the team and there’s something magical about that, feeling like you’re racing like a kid, just attacking constantly and seeing what happens. You don’t have this expectation – not from other people, but from yourself. There is magic in being a beginner and that’s a mindset I’m going to try to lean into for the next couple of years.

What motivates you?

I think of competitive sports as a way to push and discover what we’re capable of. Every athlete, every generation, takes the baton and runs as far as they can with it. For me, this era in my cycling career is all about seeing how far I can take that and truly give myself the chance to go all the way and discover what I’m capable of doing when I put my full body, mind and heart into the sport.

Is there a rider in the team or in the peloton that you find yourself wanting to pick the brain of?

It’s such a strong and deep team. We have an incredible leader in Demi [Vollering] both on and off the bike, and I’m excited to get to know her more, learn from her and support her as best I can. The special thing about being a beginner is how kind and generous everyone has been, helping me understand the ropes. Simple things like what time we go to the race, where to line up for signing on, all these things that aren’t a part of mountain biking.

You’re already a champion, but do you feel any nerves or apprehension about making this move to the road?

Absolutely! This has been an exhilarating and terrifying jump. One of the goals in making such an aggressive and quick transition was to push me outside of my comfort zone. I certainly have done that.

There’s a quote that really applies here from [American artist] Georgia O’Keeffe: ‘I’ve been absolutely terrified every moment of my life and I’ve never let it keep me from doing a single thing that I wanted to do.’

So much can be intimidating about road cycling. It’s a dangerous and aggressive sport that I think people really can’t appreciate on TV. But what makes life interesting is going after those goals that scare you a little bit.

We’re speaking at the Tour de France Femmes. You’re not racing, but are you soaking everything in?

It’s been incredible to support the team and see behind the scenes how hard everyone works, from the riders to the staff to every single person that’s involved. It’s an insane number of people. It’s very inspiring.

A key ambition of this race is inspiring younger people. Do you see yourself as a role model who younger people can look up to?

I hope to be. The ability to inspire the next generation to go further and dream bigger than we did is a huge part of the motivation to keep pushing and doing things that scare me.

What does a dream road career look like for you?

I don’t know that I can pinpoint it yet. Right now the goal is experience, and when that’s your goal, it makes it really fun to pursue something because you can learn from anything. Experiences of failure, of success, of overwhelm… I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it.

When I’m finished with my career I want to have given 100% of what I’m capable of, then having peace with that and taking that mentality into whatever I do next.
